subject: Control of queueing behaviour by arrival?

messages.author: 7840f0c79a42cce9
messages.subject: Control of queueing behaviour by arrival?
parts:
Hi,

 I'm still working on my hospital model - data now fully prepared and getting stuck into the r-simmer side of things.

 Is there any way to turn on and off queueing by arrival or during a seize activity? renege_in() doesn't seem to do quite what I want - though there may be a workaround I haven't thought of.

 My use case:

 Patient arrives in hospital and seizes a bed on the admission ward.

 I'd like them to try to seize a bed on the surgical ward, and enter a queue if one isn't immediately available. Once they successfully seize that, they'll release the admission ward bed and start a timeout for their stay.

 Once they're on the surgical ward, if they're dropped (either by pre-emption or reduction in capacity) I don't want them to enter the surgical ward's queue as a patient needs at least one bed seized at all times. (in this case they should "roll down" and seize a bed on a different - less appropriate - ward, which I'm expecting to use handle_unfinished for).

 I can't just reduce the surgical ward queue to zero because there will be other patients who need to seize a bed (but have one on the admissions ward so don't mind queueing)

 My current best-guess at a workaround is that in the event of a failed seize it's repeated every few hours, though this results in a fairly random queue.

 Does anyone have any better ideas?

thanks!

tom

On Fri, 17 May 2019 at 10:15, Tom Lawton <t...@t-lawton.org> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I'm still working on my hospital model - data now fully prepared and
> getting stuck into the r-simmer side of things.
>
> Is there any way to turn on and off queueing by arrival or during a
> seize activity? renege_in() doesn't seem to do quite what I want -
> though there may be a workaround I haven't thought of.

Not sure what you mean by "turning on and off queueing by arrival",
but note that you also have renege_if, which is basically the same as
renege_in, but based on a signal instead of a timeout.

> My use case:
>
> Patient arrives in hospital and seizes a bed on the admission ward.
>
> I'd like them to try to seize a bed on the surgical ward, and enter a
> queue if one isn't immediately available. Once they successfully seize
> that, they'll release the admission ward bed and start a timeout for
> their stay.
>
> Once they're on the surgical ward, if they're dropped (either by
> pre-emption or reduction in capacity) I don't want them to enter the
> surgical ward's queue as a patient needs at least one bed seized at
> all times. (in this case they should "roll down" and seize a bed on a
> different - less appropriate - ward, which I'm expecting to use
> handle_unfinished for).
>
> I can't just reduce the surgical ward queue to zero because there
> will be other patients who need to seize a bed (but have one on the
> admissions ward so don't mind queueing)
>
> My current best-guess at a workaround is that in the event of a
> failed seize it's repeated every few hours, though this results in a
> fairly random queue.
>
> Does anyone have any better ideas?

You can do the following. You set the surgical ward queue to zero
initially, and set up a reject trajectory in that seize. In that
reject trajectory, you just increase the queue capacity in one unit
and retry (rollback to seize). Of course, when a patient seizes the
surgical ward, it decreases the queue capacity. In this way, the queue
size is always equal to the number of patients waiting.

What happens if a patient being served in the surgical ward gets
preempted for some reason? It is automatically dropped, because there
is no room in the queue according to our setup above, and it is
catched in handle_unfinished.

Does this make sense?

Iñaki

On Fri, May 17, 2019 at 3:58 PM Tom Lawton <t...@t-lawton.org> wrote:
On Fri, May 17, 2019 at 3:21 PM Iñaki Ucar <iu...@fedoraproject.org> wrote:

> You can do the following. You set the surgical ward queue to zero
> initially, and set up a reject trajectory in that seize. In that
> reject trajectory, you just increase the queue capacity in one unit
> and retry (rollback to seize). Of course, when a patient seizes the
> surgical ward, it decreases the queue capacity. In this way, the queue
> size is always equal to the number of patients waiting.

The model is mostly built (apart from the renege issues I've mentioned). I've implemented your suggestion, but with the full model I'm struggling with what looks on the surface like some kind of (rare) race condition.
It's only happening twice in the first 12,000 patients I'm putting through the system, but is it possible for an arrival to enter the queue spot intended for another arrival using your method above?

ie Arrival A has increased the queue size for itself, but Arrival B's seize is processed in between A's set_queue_size and A's seize, so B enters the queue instead.

I can't tell whether r-simmer multitasks in this way; but I'm ending up with a couple of my patients disappearing down handle_unfinished without any ward bed decreases (they're not implemented yet) - is this possible? If so, any suggestions on avoiding it?

thanks,

tom

messages.author: 7840f0c79a42cce9
messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Control of queueing behaviour by arrival?
parts: On Fri, Jul 19, 2019 at 10:46 AM Tom Lawton <t...@t-lawton.org> wrote:
is it possible for an arrival to enter the queue spot intended for another arrival using your method above?

I've done a bit more investigation - it appears that:

Arrival A tries to seize ward and is rejected
Arrival A increases queue size on ward
Arrival A tries to seize ward again
<time>
Arrival A successfully seizes ward (so there is now a free queue spot which needs decreasing)
Arrival B tries to seize ward and enters queue (as Arrival A hasn't decreased the queue size yet)
Arrival A decreases queue size
Arrival B is dropped into handle_unfinished

Arrival A has:
    set_queue_size_selected(1,mod="+") %>%
    seize_selected() %>%
    set_queue_size_selected(-1,mod="+") %>%

So I don't know what else I can do to avoid this race.

tom

parts:
Sorry - should have made clear that this is the issue I'm having that I've solved with the "willqueue" boolean.

What's the failure of backward compatibility? As far as I can see (though I've not tested extensively) if willqueue is left out then the behaviour is as previous. Happy to tweak it to avoid issues as I'm presently using it and it seems to solve the race (but bear in mind my C++ experience!) 

Tom
